run.userPrompt:
A machinery producer sources a critical precision component from a single supplier that holds unique tooling and process know-how; qualifying an alternative would take 18 months and significant engineering effort. The supplier has recently been acquired by a competitor's parent company, raised prices twice, and slipped on delivery dates. Redesigning the product to use a different component is possible but would delay the next product generation.

Formulate a supply risk strategy for the critical component. Weigh dual-sourcing, strategic inventory, contractual protections, partial vertical integration, and product redesign; recommend a portfolio of actions with timeline and cost logic, and define the triggers that would escalate from mitigation to full independence from the supplier.

agentResponses.content:
Let me start, again, slightly to the side.

The facts as given describe a procurement problem. I'd read them as a competitive one. A competitor's parent now owns the only source of a component you cannot quickly replace, and since then your prices have gone up twice and your deliveries have slipped. That may be nothing — acquisitions are chaotic, ERP migrations wreck delivery performance, new owners rebase prices as a matter of routine. Or it may be the opening moves of something more deliberate, executed slowly enough to be deniable.

You should want to know which, and you can find out reasonably cheaply. Are the slips affecting all their customers or only you? Has their sister company's lead time changed? Did the price rise apply across the book or was yours special? Who left the business after the deal, and where did they go? Three or four conversations with people who used to work there, and a quiet word with another of their customers, will tell you more than a quarter of formal supplier reviews.

But — and this is the point I'd make before any of the analysis — the answer barely changes what you do next. If it's integration chaos, you're exposed to incompetence. If it's strategy, you're exposed to intent. The exposure is identical in shape and you must retire it either way. The diagnosis affects only your tone and your timeline, not your direction. So I wouldn't wait for it.

**The thing to fix in the first week, which costs nothing**

Your forecasts, volume plans, and probably your product roadmap currently flow into a company owned by your competitor. Whatever else happens, that stops. Rolling forecasts only, no roadmap visibility, no early engagement on the next generation, drawings under tighter control, and a review of what they already hold. Also worth establishing, urgently: who legally owns the tooling. If you funded it, you may have removal or transfer rights that nobody has looked at in years. If you didn't, that's the first thing to try to buy.

This is free, it's reversible, and it's the only element of this that has no downside. Everything else involves paying for something.

**How I'd frame the money**

Don't price these actions against the component spend. Price them against the exposure — the gross margin on every machine that cannot ship without this part, per month of interruption. That number is almost certainly one or two orders of magnitude larger than the component's annual cost, and once it's on a page the arguments about the cost of a second source tend to resolve themselves quickly. Everything below is an insurance premium. The question is only what fraction of the exposure you're willing to pay annually, and my instinct is that a business in this position should be comfortable paying a good deal more than it currently does.

**The portfolio, in the order the clock demands**

*Inventory, immediately.* This is the only lever that works in weeks rather than quarters, and its sole purpose is to buy the time the other levers need. Size it to bridge the gap between a hard stop and a qualified alternative — which, given eighteen months, is uncomfortable. You will probably not be able to afford full cover. Get to six months if you can, on the highest-margin and longest-lead configurations first, and accept that this is a partial hedge. Note the awkwardness: an unexplained order surge is a signal, and the recipient can read. Decide in advance what story accompanies it — a demand upswing, a service-stock rebuild — or accept the signal deliberately. What you shouldn't do is send it accidentally.

*Contract, in parallel.* You have less leverage than you'd like, which argues for offering something. A multi-year volume commitment is worth real money to them; trade it for a price cap, an on-time delivery undertaking with consequences that bite, capacity allocation guarantees expressed as a share of their line, last-time-buy rights on ninety days' notice, and tooling escrow or outright transfer. Change-of-control protection is a horse that's bolted, but write it in anyway for the next one.

Here is the more useful part: their *response* to this proposal is diagnostic. A supplier behaving commercially will negotiate. A supplier being steered by an owner who'd prefer you to struggle will find reasons not to commit to allocation, or to tooling access, or to any multi-year price certainty. You'll learn more from three weeks of that negotiation than from a year of scorecards.

*Qualification of a second source, starting now, not at a trigger.* Eighteen months is too long to hold in reserve. Start it in the next quarter and treat it as an option purchase, not as a decision to switch. The engineering effort is real, but it is a known, bounded, budgetable cost, and it is small against a delayed product generation or a stopped line.

Two refinements. First, a qualified-but-idle source decays — people leave, processes drift, the relationship goes cold. Give the second source a token but genuine annual volume, on a spares line or a variant, so the qualification stays live. Second, and this is where I'd spend some creativity: you are not the only customer facing this. Others buying from the same supplier now have the same owner. There may be a way to share the cost of standing up an alternative — jointly funding tooling at an independent shop, a shared qualification programme. Unusual, occasionally awkward, and very cheap relative to doing it alone.

*Partial vertical integration, as the fallback that makes the others credible.* Not building a plant. The realistic version is owning the tooling and placing it with a contract manufacturer, or acquiring a small specialist with the process knowledge, or — bluntly — hiring the three or four people in whose heads the know-how actually lives. Process expertise is rarely as embedded in equipment as the incumbent would like you to believe. I'd keep this at the level of a live, costed, named-target plan rather than an action, until a trigger fires. Its value in the meantime is that it is the reason your negotiating position isn't hollow.

*Redesign, scheduled rather than panicked.* I would not delay the next generation. I would instead insist that the generation after it, and every architecture review from now on, treats single-source dependency as a design constraint — a specified interface that admits more than one component. That's the permanent cure, and it's cheap when done at the drawing stage and ruinous when done under duress. Keep a design-out study alive as a shelved, ready-to-execute project, refreshed annually. Slow-cook it.

**Triggers**

The value of writing these down now is that the people writing them aren't yet invested in the relationship. Later, everyone will be. I'd make them mechanical and unarguable, and I'd give one named person the authority to fire them without convening anything.

Escalate to funding full independence — vertical integration or accelerated design-out, at whatever it costs — on any one of:

- A third price increase, or cumulative increases beyond a defined threshold, without a cost basis you can verify.
- On-time delivery below an agreed floor for three consecutive months, or a single allocation event where their sister company is served ahead of you.
- Refusal, or indefinite stalling, on tooling escrow, capacity allocation, or a multi-year price mechanism.
- Any lead-time extension beyond the point where your inventory buffer no longer bridges to a qualified alternative — this one is arithmetic, and worth recalculating monthly.
- Departure of the key process people at the supplier, or the transfer of your tooling to another of their sites.
- Any evidence, however soft, that commercially sensitive information has travelled to the competitor.

That last one I'd treat as decisive on its own. And if it comes to it, a monopoly supplier newly owned by a competitor, degrading service to that competitor's rival, is not only a commercial problem. There may be leverage in the merger conditions or in competition law. I wouldn't reach for it early — it converts a negotiation into a war — but it belongs in the drawer.

**Governance**

One owner, senior enough to spend, with engineering, procurement and legal reporting into the effort rather than around it. Not a procurement initiative with engineering support; the engineering is the hard part. Monthly, brief, evidence-based. And whoever runs it should not be the person whose relationship with this supplier goes back fifteen years — that person is valuable, and should be in the room, but not holding the pen.

One last thought, offered lightly. The most likely failure here isn't that you choose wrong. It's that prices stabilise, deliveries recover for two quarters, the second-source programme starts to look like an expense with no return, and someone sensible proposes deferring it. That's the moment the strategy dies. Which is why the triggers need to be written down now, and why the second source needs a small standing volume rather than a place on a shelf. Dependencies don't reassert themselves dramatically. They just quietly stop being urgent.
